title: ML Inference Senior Engineer: Hire Campaign + Simulated Interview Lab
summary: Compact hiring campaign and evaluation lab for a Senior ML Inference Engineer focused on production model serving, latency optimization, and cross-functional runbook ownership. Purpose: streamline sourcing, create repeatable interview signals tied to job-critical outcomes, and produce a first-30-day onboarding pathway that verifies ramp metrics.
hiring_plan: Goal: hire 1 Senior ML Inference Engineer (IC4/IC5-equivalent) to join serving-runtime within 8 weeks. High-level phases: 1) Sourcing & screening (week 0-2) - prioritize candidates with production inference experience (quantization, batching, kernel-level profiling), strong debugging story; 2) Technical interview loop & simulation lab (week 2-5) - combination of take-home micro-sim and two-hour onsite; 3) Offer & negotiation (week 5-6); 4) Start & first-30-day ramp plan (week 6-12). Interview panel: hiring manager (serving runtime lead), 1 applied-ML engineer, 1 infra/SRE engineer, 1 product owner (console/rollouts), and 1 people-ops interviewer for compensation/culture fit. Screen criteria: must meet minimum years of experience with GPU-backed inference (2+ yrs preferred), demonstrable latency tuning outcomes, on-call/incident participation. Score threshold for onsite invite: >=70% on phone screen rubric or exceptional take-home. Diversity sourcing notes: include outreach to ML systems meetups, post-job at conferences, and leverage internal referral bonus window. Time-to-offer target: 28 calendar days from initial screening. Hiring budget: target comp band IC4-IC5; include sign-on clawback period and hiring approval ticket JIRA-MLINF-HIRE-22.
interview_rubric:
Purpose: transform qualitative signals into measurable outcomes. Use a 5-point scale per area (1 = poor, 5 = exceptional). Areas and what to look for:

- System Design for Serving (weight 30%): evaluates ability to design a high-throughput, low-latency serving stack. Look for: tradeoffs between shard vs replicated model serving, cache strategies (prefix/KV), batching strategies, model variant routing, failure domains, and rollout safety. Example good signal: proposes KV cache warmup + selective prefix caching and explains consistency impact.

- Performance Diagnosis & Optimization (weight 25%): ability to profile (NVTX/torch.profiler-like), identify kernel-bound vs memory-bound hotspots, propose quantization/compilation strategies, and reason about latency P50/P95 tradeoffs under batching. Good signal: uses end-to-end tracing, gives concrete micro-optimization steps with expected impact (e.g., fused attention kernel reduces 90th percentile by ~15%).

- Debugging & Incident Experience (weight 15%): asks clarifying questions about previous incidents, demonstrates postmortem ownership, and describes mitigation playbooks. Good signal: led an incident, wrote a rollback+fallback policy, iterated on metrics to prevent recurrence.

- Coding Exercise (weight 15%): short pair-programming to implement a minimal KV cache with TTL semantics and unit tests or to fix a concurrency bug in a simplified batching scheduler. Evaluate for correctness, edge cases, testing, and communication.

- Cross-functional Communication & Product Sense (weight 10%): ability to translate performance tradeoffs to product decisions and costs; communicate roadmap tradeoffs to product/console teams.

- Culture & Collaboration (weight 5%): proactive mentorship, documentation habits, willingness to participate in on-call rotations.

Scoring guidance: sum(weighted scores) -> pass if >=70%. For hires above threshold consider reference check for scale projects. Panel calibration: run mock-grade with existing senior engineer to normalize scoring.

Calibration anchors (examples):
- 5 in Performance Diagnosis: candidate describes a real profiling session, reproducible benchmark, and implemented a kernel/quantization change with measurable improvement in production or staging.
- 3 average: candidate can reason well but lacks production follow-through or concrete impact numbers.
- 1 poor: guesses or lacks fundamentals about where GPU time is spent.
simulated_lab_description: Two-part lab designed to surface the candidate's production instincts and ability to operate under constraints. Part A (take-home micro-sim, 48 hours): candidate receives a small synthetic model and a simulated traffic generator. Tasks: 1) run a latency sweep across sequence lengths and batch sizes, 2) produce a short report (max 2 pages) with bottleneck hypothesis and 2 low-risk mitigations with expected numeric impact, 3) optionally include a small code patch that implements a caching policy or a lightweight batching scheduler. Evaluation rubric: clarity of experiment design, correctness of conclusions, and pragmatic mitigations. Part B (onsite lab, 120 minutes, live): 1) 30-min design whiteboard: design a fallback policy that routes to a smaller quantized model when P95 latency exceeds threshold, including data consistency implications; 2) 60-min debugging pair: provided with a failing mini-benchmark and logs showing tail latency spikes tied to KV cache misses; candidate walks through hypothesis, writes a fix (or pseudo-fix) and discusses monitoring; 3) 30-min cultural/product discussion. Dangerous anti-patterns to flag: overfitting to synthetic microbenchmarks without estimating production signal, ignoring cold-start and cache-warm semantics. Timing and logistics: take-home sent after phone screen; onsite scheduled only after take-home meets baseline quality or phone screen score >=75%.
onboarding_checklist: Objective: get the new hire to 1) be able to own a single inference-serving route end-to-end, 2) independently diagnose an introduced latency regression, and 3) ship a small latency/quality improvement within 30 days. Week 0 (pre-start): provision laptop access, dev VPN, cloud creds, intro doc with high-level architecture map, assign mentor. Week 1: orientation + shadowing: walkthrough serving runtime repo, run local end-to-end example, read past 3 postmortems, pair on a low-risk issue. Week 2: benchmarking & profiling: run provided latency sweep harness, reproduce a known latency regression in staging, submit a short incident-style note summarizing findings. Week 3: small ownership: pick a low-risk perf task from backlog (e.g., reduce serialization overhead in RPC path), propose implementation and rollout plan, implement PR with tests and perf comparison. Week 4: rollout and validation: coordinate canary rollout with console, observe metrics, complete runbook updates, present 30-day deck to team with lessons and next steps. Success metrics: able to independently push a canary, reduce P95 by measurable delta on assigned route, and update runbook. Mentorship & checkpoints: weekly 1:1 with manager, bi-weekly sync with mentor, and 30-day hire review with product and SRE reps.
acceptance_criteria: Must-haves before offer acceptance: 1) panel score >=70% with no area scored 1 on critical categories (System Design and Performance Diagnosis); 2) at least one reference confirming production ownership; 3) compensation band alignment and security clearance (if applicable). For final sign-off, hiring manager, applied-ML lead, and people-ops must approve. Post-offer conditions: successful background check and signed offer letter. For internal transfers add manager-to-manager knowledge transfer checklist.
escalation_and_operational-readiness: Runbook items to be delivered before week 4: - playbook for latency regression triage (checklist + dashboards), - immediate rollback switch and model-variant fallback config, - key SLI/metric definitions and alert thresholds. On-call readiness: shadow on-call for 2 rotations (observe), pass a brief scenario quiz (documented), and complete an incident postmortem drill. If candidate lacks on-call experience, schedule additional ramp weeks before full on-call ownership.
notes: Notes to self: 1) tighten take-home harness to restrict environmental variance (provide docker image), 2) create rubric snippets for recruiting to use in screeners, 3) coordinate with Console team to give candidate access to a read-only dashboard for the onsite lab. Outstanding questions: decide whether to require a quantitative impact number in take-home report or accept well-reasoned approximations; align legal on any IP language for take-home code. Known risks: top candidates may decline due to counteroffers—use fast-track compensation approvals for finalists.
